extracted.intended_audience: donors, nonprofit leaders, activists, and the general public interested in philanthropy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to judge and reward charitable organizations — arguing for evaluation based on accomplishments and big goals rather than minimizing expenses. Aimed at shifting donor and public norms about overhead and investment in nonprofits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reward low spending over results
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many nonprofits ... are rewarded for how little they spend -- not for what they get done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion cautions against using low overhead as the primary metric of charity quality. Instead, evaluators and donors should examine outcomes and accomplishments. Anti-pattern: choosing organizations primarily because they report minimal administrative or fundraising costs, irrespective of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward big goals and big accomplishments even with big expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of equating frugality with morality, he asks us to start rewarding charities for their big goals and big accomplishments (even if that comes with big expenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and accept that effective scale, ambitious programs, and necessary investments (e.g., staffing, marketing, infrastructure) can require substantial spending. Evaluation should consider whether expenses enable greater impact, not penalize organizations for necessary investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge the double standard in how we judge charities
rubrics_metrics.description: Activist and fundraiser Dan Pallotta calls out the double standard that drives our broken relationship to charities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broader normative criterion urges a reframing of charitable evaluation norms: identify and correct biases that moralize thriftiness and stigmatize investment or risk-taking in the nonprofit sector. Practical implication: shift donor expectations, metrics, and public narratives toward measuring effectiveness and outcomes rather than moral judgments about spending.
